title.narrative: Output 7.5. Increased capacity of Member States to develop fair and effective labour migration frameworks, institutions and services to protect migrant workers

description.narrative: 4,922 (1,484 Female) migrant workers benefited from migrant worker resource center services provided by the Malaysian Trades Union Congress (MTUC), Tenaganita, Persatuan Sahabat Wanita (PSWS) and Migrant Care. This included counselling, case management and legal aid, training, organizing and community outreach activities. Through efforts by the International Domestic Workers Federation IDWF, in collaboration with Indonesian and Philippine migrant associations, 332 women migrant domestic workers increased their capacity to organise and to advocate for the expansion of social security benefits and rights to freedom of association. Migrant workers have improved access to information on remittance service providers and market data, financial education, and how to calculate overtime and due wages through dissemination of the SaverAsia platfoms (website, mobile app) among migrant workers from Cambodia, Indonesian, Myanmar and the Philippines as well as the expansion of the platforms into Bengali and Nepali languages. Within the biennium, the SaverAsia platforms generated 112,511 user sessions from 73,463 users in Malaysia, and 824 migrant workers (W: 336, M: 488) benefitted from community training sessions on SaverAsia services. 240 employers improved their ability to investigate sexual violence and harassment complaints, especially by women migrant workers, in the world of work based on tools developed and capacity building activities conducted by the Malaysian Employers Federation. Over 50% of the Sabah Labour Inspectorate improved their capacity in carrying out inspections and conducting worker interviews with particular focus on the issues of migrant workers, forced labour, child labour, and violence and harassment. With support from Australia, European Union (EU), and United States (US), the ILO signed implementation agreements with MTUC, PSWS and Migrant Care to operate Migrant Worker Resource Centers (MRCs). The ILO has also continued to provide trainings to MRC staff on M&E and financial reporting and organizational development, as well as mainstreaming issues of gender, violence, harassment and trafficking into their service delivery strategies. With support from the EU, the ILO continued its collaboration with the International Domestic Workers Federation to strengthen migrant worker organizing in Malaysia and build the capacity of Indonesian and Philippine migrant domestic workers on labour rights, safe migration, organizing and relevant Malaysian laws. The ILO, with support from Australia, Canada and the US collaborated with SaverGlobal to conduct online and community-based dissemination activities on the SaverAsia platforms among migrant workers from Cambodia, Indonesian, Myanmar and the Philippines. With support from the US, the ILO also translated the SaverAsia platforms and developed new materials for Nepalese and Bangladeshi migrant workers. ILO partnered with the Malaysian Employers Federation to develop company policy templates and guidelines to address and investigate violence and harassment in the world of work. These tools were used by MEF to train employers on international standards and national laws associated with violence and harassment, and how to apply the guidelines and policy templates in the workplace, with specific attention to women migrant workers. With support from the US, the ILO collaborated with the Ministry of Human Resources (MOHR) to train 37 labour inspectors using the "Facilitator's Manual: Training for Malaysian Inspectors on Forced Labour, Child Labour and Gender-based Discrimination, Violence and Harassment (GBVH) in the Workplace" which ILO and MOHR published in 2022.

title.narrative: 7.5.2. Number of Member States with new or improved services to protect the labour rights of migrant workers
Output 7.3. Increased capacity of Member States to set adequate wages and promote decent working time

description.narrative: The Employment (Amendment) Act 2022 (“the Amendment Act”), went into force on 1 September 2022. The 2022 amendments allowed employees in Malaysia to apply for Flexible Working Arrangements (FWA) from their employer. The Malaysian Employer’s Federation (MEF) developed a tool (Company policy template for flexible work arrangements (hours of work, days of work, and place of work)) to provide guidance on flexible working time arrangements. The guidance included the development of an online web tool to help MEF members to understand what flexible work arrangements are and how they can be implemented in a balanced manner. In addition, draft flexible working time arrangement agreements addressing issues such as flexitime and telework were developed, to provide MEF members with draft framework agreements to be used to assist employers and workers implement flexible working time arrangements in practice. The guidance tools and framework flexible working time arrangements agreements began usage in 2023 are currently being utilised by ILO constituents in Malaysia. With support from the European Union, the ILO in collaboration with the Malaysian Employers Federation (MEF) provided guidance and assistance on flexible working time arrangements (FWA) in line with the ILO Multilateral Framework on Labour Migration and standards. The Employment Amendment Act of 2022 required employers to consider requests for flexible working time arrangements. ILO provided assistance in the development of guidance materials and draft framework agreements for use by Malaysian employers and migrant workers in line with ILO standards. Online meetings between the ILO and the MEF were organised to develop the guidance materials and develop provisions of the framework agreements on FWA. The online guidance materials were reviewed, and comments were provided by ILO to ensure a balanced online presentation of FWA to meet the needs of workers and employers. In addition, the draft FWA agreements developed by the MEF were reviewed by the ILO to make sure that the agreements balanced the needs of workers and employers using such agreements. These use of these tools and agreements began in 2023.
